references.text: The context of this verse: The two disciples began to follow Jesus after John the Baptist pointed him out as "the Lamb of God" ([ref:Joh 1:35-37|John 1:35-37]).

Jesus answers, "Come and see," and they stayed with him (ἔμειναν) that day ([ref:Joh 1:39|John 1:39]). This is the direct answer to the question "Where do you live?" and shows the first fulfillment of the μένω theme.

Shortly after this verse, John again translates a Hebrew/Aramaic expression: "Messiah" means "Christ" ([ref:Joh 1:41-42|John 1:41-42]). This is part of John's pattern of translating terms for his readers.
Nicodemus comes to Jesus and calls him "Rabbi," acknowledging him as a teacher who has come from God ([ref:Joh 3:2|John 3:2]).
The crowd finds Jesus on the other side of the sea and asks, "Rabbi, when did you come here?" ([ref:Joh 6:25|John 6:25]). The same title is used again for Jesus.

Mary Magdalene calls Jesus "Rabbuni" (which means "my master/teacher") at the resurrection ([ref:Joh 20:16|John 20:16]). John also translates this Aramaic expression here for his readers, as he does in 1:38.

The Samaritans ask Jesus to stay with them, and he stayed there two days ([ref:Joh 4:40|John 4:40]). The question "Where do you live?" in 1:38 expresses a desire to be with Jesus, which is reflected in the theme of "abiding" (μένω) with Jesus throughout the Gospel of John.

Jesus says, "Abide in me, and I will abide in you" ([ref:Joh 15:4-5|John 15:4-5]). The verb μένω (abide/dwell) in the question "Where do you live?" is a key word in the Gospel of John that points to the deeper fellowship with Jesus.

Jesus warns against letting yourselves be called "Rabbi," for "one is your teacher" ([ref:Matt 23:7-8|Matthew 23:7-8]). The title "Rabbi" used by the disciples in John 1:38 is the same title Jesus later puts into perspective.
